name: Tewa
catalog_quote: all two-syllable nouns of syllable pattern CVCV and tone pattern high-high or low-low show decidedly heavier stress on the first syllable than on the second--regardless of their position in the utterance, so that the weaker stress cannot be attributed to /#/.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and every supporting phrase in the record (pp. 75-77, p. 44) are verbatim on the page images we hold of Speirs 1966; locator correct (printed p. 76 = PDF p. 82). (2) Deciding source: a 1966 PhD dissertation that Glottolog types as the language's only grammar(-sketch) and that Sutton 2014 (held, opened now) calls the best published treatment of Tewa phonology; Sutton 2014:1028 independently states stem-initial lexical stress for Kiowa-Tanoan, confirming the root-initial reading behind our 'initial, dominant not strict' coding and the the primary-stress rule. No newer grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study of Tewa stress was found (Glottolog 45 refs; Crossref; Sutton's 2014 literature review says 21st-century academic work on Rio Grande Tewa is minimal and publication-restricted).

sources.quote: p. 1028: 'As bound grammaticalized morphemes, they [pronominal proclitics] rarely bear primary lexical stress ... Since lexical stress in Kiowa-Tanoan has a tendency to fall on the first syllable of a lexical stem, we might expect the sound correspondences to be more akin to what we find word-internally and word-finally'. p. 118: Speirs 1966 'provides the best treatment of segmental and tonal phonology yet to be published'.
